sourceVerbParadigms.note: Stem change o to ue, except nosotros. Use cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several.
Reflexive verb. Use it for names of people and things.
Irregular yo form (estoy). Use estar to say where something is.
Stem change e to ie, except nosotros.
Stem change e to ie, except nosotros. Quieren is the ustedes form, used when speaking to a group.

frenchVerbParadigms.note: Source example: card 13 and Reader line 5, "Combien coûte le petit-déjeuner ?" = "How much is the breakfast?". Regular -er verb; the source o-to-ue stem-change note does not transfer. Use coûte for one thing and coûtent for several.

Source example: card 14 and Reader line 7, "Comment s'appelle ce pain ?" = "What is this bread called?". Pronominal verb, used for names of people and things. Spelling has ll in all forms except nous and vous.

Source example: card 12 and Reader line 8, "Où sont les toilettes ?" = "Where is the restroom?". Irregular. French uses être to say where something is. The Reader uses sont because les toilettes is plural.

Source example: Reader line 2, "Je vous sers" = "I am serving you."; also card 16 and Reader line 1, "Qui nous sert ?". Irregular singular stem ser-; the source e-to-ie stem-change note does not transfer.

Source example: Reader line 2, "Quel café voulez-vous ?" = "What coffee do you want?". Irregular. Voulez is the vous form, used when speaking to a group or formally; it stands for the source ustedes form quieren.

internalDomainNotes: qué/cuál: the Spanish split (source note: use cuál to choose from options) does not map one-to-one onto French. French quel covers both ¿qué café? (Reader line 2) and ¿cuál es…? (Reader line 3, card 15). Card faces 1 and 8 therefore teach the English senses what? and which? and make no claim about the Spanish distinction.
Card 1: quoi stands alone or after a preposition; que or qu'est-ce que opens a clause. Before a noun, 'what' is quel (Reader line 2).
Card 8: lequel stands alone as a pronoun; quel goes before a noun or with être. Both agree in gender and number (quelle, laquelle, quels, lesquels).
Source note on por qué (why) versus porque (because): the French counterpart is pourquoi versus parce que. Kept off the card face.
Comment s'appelle… is the French idiom for 'What is … called?'; comment otherwise means how.
Pan dulce: Mexican sweet rolls, like the shell-shaped concha (source note). Concha is treated as feminine in French: une concha.
Café de olla: Mexican coffee traditionally brewed in a clay pot, typically with cinnamon and piloncillo. Kept as an unelided loan term (le café de olla, not d'olla).
Restroom: source el baño is singular; French les toilettes is plural, so está becomes sont in card 12 and Reader lines 8 and 9.
Hotel roles: Emma and Tom are guests; Rosa is the host or server. Rosa addresses both guests, so vous is plural here.
French has no ser/estar split; être covers the source estar (location).
'11 heures' and 'à droite' are neutral details, not Mexico-specific.

cards.ownerVisibleIssue: French quoi is standalone/informal; que requires a following clause. The source Spanish qué also appears before a noun, where French uses quel. This two-face candidate must be reviewed before shown as one settled answer.
French lequel stands alone and quel needs a noun or être; gender/number variants are omitted from this card face. Source cuál and qué both map to quel in different Reader contexts.
Pan dulce is a Mexican sweet roll category including concha; literal French pain sucré may underdescribe it. Food-language review required.
